title: Famous Game Analysis + Live Chess | Moistcr1tikal / Penguinz0

moves.spoken: A famous Rubinstein brilliancy, and it opens quietly — White's d4, and Rubinstein answers d5.
A queen's-pawn opening — White develops the knight to f3.
Black plays e6, reinforcing the pawn on d5.
White mirrors with e3. The drawback of both e6 and e3 is the same — each shuts in a bishop; conservative, but not bad.
Black contests the centre with c5.
White challenges with c4.
The knight to c6.
And the knight to c3.
Now a little box of pawns forms in the centre — it looks tangled, but everything defends everything, so neither side wants to be first to flinch.
But White flinches — the capture on c5, releasing the tension.
Rubinstein recaptures, the bishop to c5.
White plays a3 — preparing something. What is it?
The idea is b4 — so Rubinstein slips in a6 first; you will see the point in a moment.
White expands with b4.
The bishop drops back to d6 — and here is the point of a6: it discourages White from harassing the knight with b5, because Black would take on b5 and blast open the a-file.
White takes on d5.
After the recapture White grabs on d5 with the knight — so why isn't this just a free pawn?
Because the move order is everything. Black takes the knight first, and if White grabs back with the queen, that queen becomes a sitting duck — the check on b4 wins it.
The bishop checks on b4, and next move the queen is snapped off. Take the pawn first, though, and it all falls apart.
Because if Black grabs the pawn first, White simply recaptures the bishop — with knight or pawn — and just wins the pawn straight back. Order matters.
So instead White fianchettoes the bishop to b2, Black castles, and the queen comes to d2.
In fact White never captured on d5 at all — he just left the d-pawn alone and developed: the bishop to b2, castling, the queen to d2.
Rubinstein plays the queen to e7, connecting the rooks.
White develops the bishop to d3. Now look at Black's light bishop, still back on c8 — can it be developed just as actively as White's, and all by force?
The goal is to get that bishop out to b7 with tempo — but you cannot just fire out b5 first.
Because White would simply take the free pawn.
So first Black takes on c4, luring the bishop out — don't be so reluctant to trade in order to get things done.
The bishop recaptures on c4...
...and NOW b5, hitting the bishop.
White has to waste a move retreating the bishop to d3.
And the bishop swings out to b7 — developed actively and with tempo, reaching a near-symmetrical position but with Black a step ahead.

One small drawback remains — that white queen sitting on d2. Can we make it uncomfortable? Yes: a rook to d8 pins the bishop against it down the open file, and parking the queen on d2 turns out to be a real mistake. It sets up the Greek-gift idea too — both bishops x-ray White's king — but first the knight must step out, to e5 offering a trade, to clear the way for the sacrifice.
